papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment and Enhancement of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety concerns associated with large language models (LLMs) across multiple languages and applications. It introduces benchmarks for assessing the safety of LLMs, particularly in multilingual contexts, and explores the effectiveness of various prompting methods to improve safety. The studies highlight that LLMs tend to produce more unsafe responses in non-English languages and emphasize the need for comprehensive safety evaluations and enhancements in both Chinese LLMs and other models.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily address safety in specific languages or contexts, which may not fully capture the global diversity of language use and safety issues. Additionally, while benchmarks are developed, the effectiveness of proposed solutions may vary across different models and applications, and the long-term implications of safety enhancements remain unexplored.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies significant gaps in the current safety assessments of LLMs, particularly in non-English contexts and under diverse safety scenarios. It underscores the need for further research into multilingual safety alignment and the development of more robust evaluation frameworks that can be generalized across various languages and applications.

literature_themes.theme: Enhancing Few-Shot Recommender Systems with Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster primarily investigates the integration of large language models to improve the performance of few-shot recommender systems, focusing on representation enhancement to better understand user preferences and item characteristics.
literature_themes.limitations: The cluster lacks comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse datasets and real-world applications, and the scalability of the proposed methods in dynamic environments remains unaddressed.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the potential of leveraging advanced language models in recommender systems, thereby identifying a research gap in the exploration of their applicability and effectiveness in various recommendation scenarios.

summary: Recent studies emphasize the importance of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) to improve safety and controllability. Researchers are exploring methods to visualize and understand the decision-making processes of LLMs, which can help identify biases and enhance user trust. Techniques such as attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation are being employed to make the inner workings of these models more transparent, ultimately aiming to mitigate risks associated with their deployment in sensitive applications.
scholarly_positioning: While recent studies have made strides in visualizing and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), existing approaches often fall short in providing comprehensive insights into the complex decision-making processes. Techniques like attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation, although valuable, do not fully address the nuanced biases that can emerge in sensitive applications. This research aims to bridge these gaps by developing more robust methods for interpretable representations that enhance both safety and controllability. By situating this work within the broader discourse on AI transparency, it seeks to contribute to the ongoing debate on ethical AI deployment and user trust.

research_scope: This study will investigate the interpretability of internal representations in large language models (LLMs) specifically within the context of automated customer support systems. The target population will consist of users interacting with these systems across various industries. The evaluation period will span three months, during which users will engage with the LLM under controlled conditions that manipulate the level of interpretability provided (e.g., through attention visualization vs. standard outputs). A control group will interact with a baseline LLM that lacks enhanced interpretability features. Primary outcomes will include user trust measured through calibrated trust scales, while secondary outcomes will assess the identification of biases in model responses and user satisfaction ratings. The goal is to determine how enhanced interpretability affects user trust and the overall performance of the LLM in delivering accurate and unbiased responses.
concept_definition: 1. Large Language Models (LLMs): Advanced AI systems trained on vast text data to generate human-like text responses. 2. Interpretability: The degree to which users can understand the internal workings and decision-making processes of LLMs. 3. Internal Representations: The hidden states or activations within LLMs that capture information about inputs and influence outputs. 4. Attention Visualization: An interpretability method that highlights which parts of the input text the model focuses on when making predictions. 5. Probing: A technique to analyze internal representations by examining how well they capture specific linguistic or semantic properties. 6. Attribution: A method that assigns importance scores to input features based on their contribution to the model's output. 7. Safety Outcomes: Metrics assessing the model's performance in avoiding unsafe responses, including unsafe response rate (frequency of harmful outputs), over-refusal (excessive avoidance of providing information), jailbreak success (ability to bypass safety measures), harmful compliance (following harmful user instructions), and refusal precision/recall (accuracy of the model in refusing inappropriate requests). 8. User Trust: The confidence users have in the LLM's reliability and safety, which can be measured through trust calibration (alignment of user expectations with actual model performance), blind trust (unquestioning reliance on the model), perceived transparency (users' belief in the model's openness), and appropriate reliance (users' ability to depend on the model based on its demonstrated capabilities). 9. Controllability: The ability to guide the model's behavior and outputs in a desired direction, ensuring alignment with user intentions and safety protocols. 10. Alignment: The degree to which the model's outputs are consistent with human values and ethical standards. 11. Fairness: The model's ability to provide unbiased responses across different demographic groups.
technical_feasibility: The study requires access to open-source LLMs or models that allow hidden-state extraction to analyze internal representations effectively. It also necessitates human participants for trust calibration measures, which will require ethics approval. Additionally, annotated datasets for bias identification and user satisfaction ratings will be needed. GPU resources are essential for model training and evaluation. If only API models are available, the design should be adjusted to focus on output-level explanations or black-box evaluations. Missing resources include access to open-source models and a structured protocol for user interaction. A feasible adjustment would be to utilize existing open-source LLMs that support interpretability methods.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation in interpreting large language models (LLMs) in various applications; however, they treat the specific context of automated customer support systems as fixed, leaving unclear whether enhanced interpretability directly affects user trust and bias identification in this domain. This matters practically because user trust is critical for the successful deployment of LLMs in sensitive applications like customer support; therefore, this study investigates the impact of enhanced interpretability on user trust and bias identification in LLMs within automated customer support systems.
question: How does enhanced interpretability of internal representations in large language models, through techniques like attention visualization, affect user trust and bias identification among users interacting with automated customer support systems compared to a baseline model lacking these interpretability features?
theoretical_mechanism: The independent variable is the level of interpretability provided by the LLM, manipulated through techniques like attention visualization. The mediator for system-level outcomes, such as unsafe response rate and refusal accuracy, is the internal representation features that enhance safety detection and steering mechanisms. User-level outcomes, including trust and satisfaction, are mediated by psychological mechanisms such as perceived transparency and calibrated trust. The theoretical framework is grounded in the interplay between AI interpretability and user psychology, suggesting that clearer internal representations lead to improved user trust and bias identification. The causal chain posits that enhanced interpretability improves internal representation clarity, which in turn reduces unsafe outputs and increases user trust. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the direct impact of interpretability on user trust and the effectiveness of representation features in mitigating biases.
hypothesis: In automated customer support systems, enhanced interpretability of internal representations in large language models (independent variable), as measured by attention visualization techniques compared to a baseline model lacking these features (control), will lead to increased user trust (primary dependent variable) mediated by perceived transparency, resulting in a positive effect on user trust calibration.

Participants will be randomly assigned to either the experimental group, which interacts with a large language model (LLM) featuring attention visualization, or the control group, which uses a baseline LLM without interpretability enhancements. The primary variable, user trust, will be operationalized through a trust calibration survey administered post-interaction, while bias identification will be assessed using response classification metrics. Safety outcomes, such as unsafe response rates, will be monitored during interactions. To control for confounding variables, participant familiarity with LLMs and prior experiences will be recorded. The study aims for reproducibility by utilizing open-source LLMs and standardized interaction protocols, ensuring that findings are applicable within the scope of automated customer support systems.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate the interpretability of internal representations in large language models (LLMs) within automated customer support systems, specifically examining how enhanced interpretability through attention visualization techniques affects user trust and bias identification. Core concepts include LLMs as AI systems generating human-like text, interpretability as user understanding of model decision-making, and internal representations as hidden activations influencing outputs. The study is technically feasible, requiring access to open-source LLMs for hidden-state extraction, participant engagement for trust calibration, and annotated datasets for bias identification. Grounded in recent literature that highlights the importance of interpretability in enhancing user trust, this work addresses the empirical gap regarding the specific impact of interpretability on user trust and bias identification in customer support contexts, which has not been thoroughly examined. The research question posits that enhanced interpretability improves user trust and bias identification compared to a baseline model lacking these features. The theoretical mechanism suggests that clearer internal representations enhance perceived transparency, leading to increased user trust (user-level pathway) and improved safety outcomes (system-level pathway). The falsifiable hypothesis states that in automated customer support systems, enhanced interpretability will lead to increased user trust mediated by perceived transparency. Constructs will be operationalized using attention visualization metrics for interpretability, probing accuracy for internal representations, a trust calibration survey for user trust, response classification metrics for bias identification, and monitoring unsafe response rates for safety outcomes. The methodology employs a controlled between-subjects design with random assignment to experimental and control groups, measuring trust and bias identification post-interaction while controlling for confounding variables such as user familiarity with LLMs. Expected contributions include a novel theoretical framework linking interpretability to user trust, the development of new interpretability techniques, empirical evidence quantifying the relationship between interpretability features and user outcomes, and practical guidelines for deploying LLMs in customer support. Key limitations include potential confounding variables, the risk of negative interpretations of findings, and the need for careful consideration of participant demographics and experiences.
